title: The Deadly Poppy Field, part 2
attribution: From The Wonderful Wizard of Oz by L. Frank Baum (1900), via Project Gutenberg, in reading order.
body: “Good-bye!” he called after them, and they were very sorry to leave him. Indeed, the Tin Woodman began to cry, but fortunately remembered that he might rust, and so dried his tears on Dorothy’s apron.
Of course this was a bad thing for the Scarecrow.

“I am now worse off than when I first met Dorothy,” he thought. “Then, I was stuck on a pole in a cornfield, where I could make-believe scare the crows, at any rate. But surely there is no use for a Scarecrow stuck on a pole in the middle of a river. I am afraid I shall never have any brains, after all!”
Down the stream the raft floated, and the poor Scarecrow was left far behind. Then the Lion said:
“Something must be done to save us. I think I can swim to the shore and pull the raft after me, if you will only hold fast to the tip of my tail.”

So he sprang into the water, and the Tin Woodman caught fast hold of his tail. Then the Lion began to swim with all his might toward the shore. It was hard work, although he was so big; but by and by they were drawn out of the current, and then Dorothy took the Tin Woodman’s long pole and helped push the raft to the land.

They were all tired out when they reached the shore at last and stepped off upon the pretty green grass, and they also knew that the stream had carried them a long way past the road of yellow brick that led to the Emerald City.
“What shall we do now?” asked the Tin Woodman, as the Lion lay down on the grass to let the sun dry him.
“We must get back to the road, in some way,” said Dorothy.
“The best plan will be to walk along the riverbank until we come to the road again,” remarked the Lion.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the Tin Woodman dry his tears on?
options: Dorothy's apron
The grass of the bank
His own tin arm
A leaf from the trees

questions.prompt: Per the passage, why did the Tin Woodman stop crying?
options: He remembered he might rust
The Lion told him to be quiet
The Scarecrow called out to him
The raft began to tip over

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the Lion offer to do?
options: Swim ashore and pull the raft after him
Jump to the bank and fetch help
Dive down to free the stuck pole
Carry Dorothy on his back to land

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what did the Tin Woodman hold on to?
options: The tip of the Lion's tail
The edge of the wooden raft
Dorothy's outstretched hand
His own long pushing pole

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the Lion do once they reached the shore?
options: Lay down on the grass to dry in the sun
Went to look for the yellow road
Swam straight back for the Scarecrow
Slept until the following morning

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Scarecrow think he is worse off than before?
options: On a pole in a river he cannot even pretend to scare crows
He has lost the basket Dorothy trusted him with
He can no longer see the road to the Emerald City
The water will rot the straw he is stuffed with

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, how did Dorothy help once the Lion had them out of the current?
options: She took the long pole and pushed the raft to land
She called out directions to the swimming Lion
She held Toto up so the Lion could see them
She paddled with her hands over the side

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what had the river cost them besides the Scarecrow?
options: It carried them far past the yellow brick road
It swept away the basket and the oil-can
It left them on the Wicked Witch's own bank
It broke the raft the Woodman had built

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does the Scarecrow mean by make-believe scare the crows?
options: Pretend to do it without really succeeding
Frighten them by pure accident
Do it better than any other scarecrow
Refuse to do it at all any more

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the passage?
options: The Lion swims them ashore, far off course and one friend short
The Scarecrow is pulled from his pole and back onto the raft
The travellers leave the raft and swim for the nearer bank
The Tin Woodman rusts in the river and has to be left there

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what was the Lion's swim like?
options: Hard work, even for so big a beast
Easy, because the current helped him
Impossible until the Woodman let go
Short, since the bank was near

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what plan did the Lion suggest on the shore?
options: Walk along the riverbank until they met the road
Build a second raft and cross back over
Wait where they were for the Scarecrow
Follow the river down to the witch's country

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the Scarecrow call after them?
options: Good-bye
Come back
Help me
Nothing at all

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, how did the party feel about leaving the Scarecrow?
options: Very sorry, and one of them wept over it
Relieved, since the raft rode better without him
Confident that he would free himself soon
Angry with him for pushing so hard

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the Scarecrow fear most about his position?
options: That he will never get any brains after all
That the crows will come and pull out his straw
That the river will rise and carry him off
That his friends will forget where he is

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does it mean that they were drawn out of the current?
options: Pulled clear of the fast-moving water
Rescued by someone on the bank
Lifted out of the water entirely
Turned to face back upstream

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarises the passage?
options: A rescue by swimming that lands them safe but off course
A rescue that brings the Scarecrow back to the raft
A decision to float downstream to the witch's country
A quarrel about who was to blame for the lost pole
